rv.q: Amelia Sears’s delicate revival gently fathoms its depths and demonstrates how the playwright brought his acute understanding of emotional reticence to bear on a rapidly changing society.
And yet, despite a first half drowning in a vat of viscous exposition, explaining themselves to each other and a biddable American friend, the second half is much more intriguing.
Still, it is not as monumental a play as The Deep Blue Sea, also about the disenchantments of romance, nor is it as chamber-like as some of Rattigan’s double-bills (such as Summer 1954).

And in Amelia Sears’s unfussy production of the late-period In Praise of Love at Richmond’s Orange Tree, it’s hard to see — at first, anyway — why Estonian-born Lydia tolerates a self-centred husband, Sebastian, who treats her as little more than a home help. It’s only as the backstory unfolds that we begin to sense the depth of their relationship.

An echo here of Rex, who once told his singer son he wouldn’t be going to see him in his one-man show: ‘I can’t bear to be bored.’ Directed by Amelia Sears, it’s frightfully heart on sleeve, the play’s central idea being that the great English vice is emotional repression.
It is a multi-layered and quietly powerful performance.
By the time Rowan’s Sebastian wins our sympathy with his desperate declaration of love and need at the close of the play, he has long forfeited much claim to it.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this Rattigan revival: critics praise Claire Price's performance but find the production uneven, with some moved by its emotional undercurrents and others left cold by the leads' chemistry and the play's dated restraint.
